title: The charity of the fast's end
hookLine: a small gift of food paid before the Eid prayer so the poor celebrate too

cards: Tomorrow is the feast. Somewhere tonight, a family is ironing new clothes and making sweets. And somewhere not far away, a family is wondering what there'll be to eat tomorrow at all.

It's been a month in a week on this path: a thread of moon low in the west, a meal in the dark before dawn, a date at sunset, long nights of standing, a night worth a lifetime, a fast of the tongue. Now it's almost over.
Before the feast can start, the tradition asks for one thing.

teach.h: A SA' OF DATES OR BARLEY.
teach.b: It's called zakat al-fitr, the charity of breaking the fast. A companion, Ibn Umar, describes it in Bukhari.

teach.h: ON EVERY MUSLIM, EVEN A BABY.
teach.b: The Prophet ﷺ made it obligatory: a sa' of dates or a sa' of barley, on every Muslim, free or enslaved, man or woman, young or old, paid before people go out to the Eid prayer.
A sa' was a measure of volume, about four double handfuls: two cupped hands, filled, four times. Enough food for a family's day. Notice who it's on.
Everyone, not only the wealthy, like the yearly zakat you met in camp one. The head of a household pays for each person in it, even a baby born that month. Almost everyone gives; the poorest receive.
Why? Another companion, Ibn Abbas, gives two reasons in the Sunan of Abu Dawud.
It purifies the one who fasted from any idle or hurtful talk that slipped through the month; a kind of closing apology for yesterday's lesson. And it's food for the poor.

Then the timing: paid before the prayer, it's zakat al-fitr. Paid after, it's just ordinary charity. The deadline is the point: the gift has to arrive in time for the poor to celebrate too, not the day after.
Today most Muslims give its value, often through a mosque, which buys food or passes on the money. Schools differ on whether money counts or it must be food; the Hanafi school has long allowed money.
But the aim hasn't changed in fourteen centuries.
Nobody should be hungry on the feast.

how: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslim households give zakat al-fitr for every member, a measure of staple food or, in many communities, its cash value, usually through a mosque that passes it to people in need.

o: food given by nearly all, before the Eid prayer
a share of the harvest set aside for guests
a fine paid for missing a day of fasting

games.q: what's inside the gift — tap the pairs.
p: on every Muslim, young or old

s: zakat al-fitr is only paid by the wealthy
it's on nearly every Muslim, young or old, with the head of a household paying for each member.
it must be paid before the Eid prayer
paid before, it's zakat al-fitr; after, it's ordinary charity (Abu Dawud, from Ibn Abbas).
every school requires it to be food, never money
the Hanafi school has long allowed money, and many communities give the value.

games.q: it's the morning of Eid, and you haven't paid zakat al-fitr yet. people are heading to the prayer. when does it still count?
o: only if you pay it before the prayer
games.why: before the prayer, it's zakat al-fitr; after, it counts as ordinary charity. the point is that the poor can celebrate too.

practice: Cup your two hands in front of you, as if holding grain, and fill them in your mind four times: that's a sa', food on someone's table tomorrow.
Think of one real way a meal's worth could reach someone: a food bank, a neighbor, a coworker who's struggling, a mosque's collection. If you pray, you can ask that it reach someone in time.

wordCard.voice: Zakat al-fitr. The charity at the end of the fast: food given by nearly everyone, before the Eid prayer, so the poor celebrate too. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the charity of breaking the fast; fitr shares a root with iftar.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone eats on eid. The gift has to arrive in time. A week, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1503 (Ibn Umar: a sa' of dates or barley, on every Muslim, before the prayer)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1609 (Ibn Abbas: a purification for the faster and food for the poor)
